strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem for human-centered NLP: whether interactive theme-discovery systems perform differently under different collaboration workflows. Its contribution is clearly motivated and connects NLP evaluation with qualitative research practice.

The comparison covers three substantially different approaches on a shared corpus of approximately 85,000 tweets. Evaluating consistency, cohesiveness, distinctiveness, and assignment correctness separately helps expose tradeoffs that a single aggregate measure would obscure. Fixed initial partitions within each system reduce one source of variation.

The evaluation includes substantial human involvement: 20 participants, 1,200 manually checked document–theme pairs, two evaluators with adjudication, and participant interviews. Reporting agreement and providing prompts, selected system settings, and interview questions are useful transparency measures.
weaknesses: The experimental comparison does not isolate collaboration timing. The introduction defines asynchronous collaboration as independent coding followed by joint consolidation, but Section 4 evaluates individual codebooks without describing consolidation, against codebooks produced by three-person synchronous teams. Timing is therefore confounded with team size and pooled human input. Participant allocation, reuse, ordering, and time budgets are also unspecified; 20 participants occupy 27 coder-session slots. A matched comparison incorporating consolidation, or substantially narrower claims about individual versus group coding, is needed.

The statistical evidence supporting the central claim is insufficiently justified. Tables 1–2 use unpaired t-tests without identifying the sampling unit or effective sample sizes. Each tool has only two synchronous sessions and three asynchronous sessions; theme matches share codebooks and documents. Treating these matches as independent observations would constitute pseudoreplication. Report session-level outcomes, account for dependencies, and provide uncertainty and multiple-comparison handling. The designation 'near statistically significant' does not establish an effect.

The proposed framework needs stronger validation as a measure of thematic quality. Maximum theme matching does not clearly specify directionality, repeated matches, or treatment of unmatched themes, and its behavior can depend on theme counts and granularity, which are not reported. Centroid similarities are approximately 0.94–0.98 across all configurations, making calibration particularly important. Sensitivity analyses and human assessment of thematic alignment would help establish what these scores mean beyond geometric similarity.

The correctness evaluation is not sufficiently defined. Figure 4 reports F1, but Section 5 does not explain how binary judgments of document–theme assignments yield precision and recall, or specify the averaging procedure. Uniform sampling across themes also requires an explicit estimand and weighting explanation before representing dataset-wide performance. Treatment of unassigned documents, including the 0.7–16.1% invalid-label rate in Table 4, is unclear. No uncertainty is shown. Moreover, the claimed topic-model advantage for asynchronous coding is not supported consistently by Figure 4: both conditions end near 0.50, and synchronous coding scores higher at intermediate cutoffs.

Several conclusions exceed the comparisons performed. One tool per category cannot establish that the number of available interventions causes greater benefits from synchronous discussion. Likewise, experiments with Llama 3.2 3B-Instruct on one vaccination corpus do not support general conclusions about LLM reliability or scalability. The relational system also receives stance and morality information, complicating explanations of cross-system differences. These findings should be framed as observations about the tested configurations and hypotheses for subsequent study.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful appendices. Missing details include the exact S-BERT checkpoint, participant/session mapping, final codebooks, selected prompt per session, decoding settings, and correctness-annotation instructions. Code and annotation outputs are promised without an artifact location. Appendix C also acknowledges skipped interviews and differing individual/group interview formats, but provides neither completion counts nor a qualitative analysis procedure. Together with the design and inference issues, these gaps prevent a clear Findings recommendation in the current version.
